extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in science communication (scholars, journalists, public-facing science communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review of experimental literature testing how different portrayals of uncertainty in public-facing science communication affect audience beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors. Includes a typology of uncertainty types, inclusion/coding criteria, moderators, and practical recommendations for communicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deficient uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty communicated by emphasizing a known gap in knowledge — 'known unknowns' such as lack of research or expanded problem space. Example operationalization: clauses like 'although much remains unknown and more research is still needed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deficient uncertainty has produced mixed effects in experiments (positive, negative, null) and often interacts with individual-level moderators. Use when accurately communicating limitations; expect context- and audience-dependent responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantified uncertainty such as measurement error, modeling approximations, statistical assumptions — expressed as ranges (e.g., 7–15 cm), probabilities (e.g., 65% chance), confidence intervals, or error bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across reviewed experiments technical uncertainty showed only positive or null effects (no instances of negative effects). It's a form of transparency that often increases or does not harm credibility and behavioral intentions. Prefer numerical/quantified presentations when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal of the (un)certainty in terms of collective discord or accord among experts or within the body of evidence; similar to 'disagreement,' 'conflict,' or 'controversy.' Frequently used as an experimental manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most consistent experimental pattern: consensus uncertainty is associated with negative main effects (reduced credibility, belief, intentions). The review found no instances of consensus uncertainty producing positive main effects. Use with caution — only when context and goals justify communicating expert disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal of the epistemological feature that current best understandings may change in the future ('unknown unknowns'); communicates that findings are tentative because future data/theory may change interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific uncertainty has been studied less frequently; findings are mixed (some positive, some null, occasional negative). It may be perceived as an inherent feature of science and can be acceptable to audiences if framed appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of positive vs negative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational definitions used in the review: 'negative effects' indicate a significant decrease in belief in, perceived credibility of, or intentions to follow message recommendations; 'positive effects' indicate a significant increase in these outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating experimental outcomes, classify effects according to their direction on belief, credibility, and behavioral intentions. Note that increases in risk perception or behavioral intentions may be 'positive' or 'negative' depending on the message's advocacy position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria for experimental studies
rubrics_metrics.description: To be included, a study must: portray uncertainty as an experimental manipulation (levels compared to a control with no uncertainty); be experimental (exclude non-experimental designs); have the treatment message about a science-related topic (claims made by scientists or science generally); be in a public-facing mass communication context (journalism, scientific reports, PSAs, campaigns); measure persuasive effects on beliefs, attitudes, or behaviors (exclude studies measuring correctness of comprehension); manipulate uncertainty within a single message (exclude multi-message manipulations); focus on verbal and numerical depictions (exclude visual depictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural criteria define the population of experimental studies relevant to the review. When designing new experiments or meta-analyses, match these constraints or explicitly justify deviations (e.g., interpersonal contexts, visual uncertainty representations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search procedure standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Search strategy used: Google Scholar searches combining terms ([uncertainty AND experiment AND 'science communication'] and variants), 40 separate searches, examined first 200 items per search (8,000 results total), and snowballed forward and backward citations until saturation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a reproducible, pragmatic strategy for comprehensive retrieval in this literature: limit per-search checks to where relevance drops, and use citation chaining to capture omitted works. Document cutoffs and potential gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding scheme and manifest/latent content coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding categories (Table 1) include: author/year, total N (# experiments), sample type (R, N, C, S), topics, uncertainty types (D=Deficient, T=Technical, S=Scientific, C=Consensus), main effects (labels +, -, strike for non-significant), conditional effects and moderators. The first author coded manifest and latent content and consulted the second author for ambiguities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent, pre-specified coding labels and definitions; provide access to detailed coding definitions upon request or in supplemental materials; resolve coder ambiguities via consultation or double-coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome variables to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary outcomes of interest: belief in the message, perceived credibility (trust, honesty, expertise, competence), behavioral intentions, risk perceptions; also internal certainty (one’s own level of certainty) and external certainty (perception of scientists’/experts’ level of certainty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on persuasive outcomes (attitudes, intentions, trust). The review excluded comprehension/correctness outcomes; researchers should justify outcome choices relative to study goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty as framing (framing types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing theory: framing selects aspects of perceived reality to make them salient to promote problem definitions, causal interpretations, moral evaluations, or treatment recommendations. Two fundamental message framing types are emphasis (highlighting a theme) and equivalence (logically equal but differently valenced content). Uncertainty portrayals can function as emphasis frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat uncertainty choices as framing decisions that shape which schemas and associations are activated. Consider the intended interpretive frame (emphasis vs equivalence) when constructing uncertainty language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of expression: verbal vs numerical uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty can be expressed verbally (hedges, caveats) or numerically (probabilities, ranges). van der Bles et al. (2020) found that verbal (but not numerical) expressions slightly reduced participants' own levels of certainty and trust in the message source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical/technical representations tend to have neutral or positive effects; verbal expressions may reduce perceived certainty/trust. Prefer quantified presentations for transparency, and be mindful that lexical hedges can have differential effects depending on audience literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key individual-level moderators
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent moderators of uncertainty effects include: prior worldviews and prior topic opinions (motivated reasoning/confirmation bias), trust in science and scientists (deference), perceived role of uncertainty in science (belief about whether uncertainty is natural/acceptable), and topic/context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect conditional effects: uncertainty manipulations can flip sign depending on moderators. Measure these moderators and test interactions; tailor communication strategies to audience beliefs, trust, and topic sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic and contextual sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of uncertainty often vary by topic (e.g., climate change, vaccines, GMOs) and context; some uncertainty types produced negative effects in one topic but not in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize findings across topics without caution. Evaluate uncertainty communication strategies within the specific topical and cultural context and test for topic-specific moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendations for communicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy/practice guidance from the review: 'public-facing science communicators can be encouraged that many uncertainties of science should not be shunned... portrayals of deficient, technical, or scientific uncertainties can – and often do – engender positive or neutral responses.' 'Communicators should feel confident in expressing technical uncertainty without fear of negative repercussions, but should be cautious about expressing consensus uncertainty unless it is appropriate to their context and goals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer technical (quantified) disclosures when transparency is desired; use deficient/scientific uncertainty thoughtfully; avoid highlighting expert disagreement unless necessary for accuracy or strategic goals. Tailor messaging to audience trust and prior beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and cautions in interpreting experimental findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Identified limitations include publication bias, many included studies with very small samples (risk of non-replicable findings), search/inclusion criteria possibly excluding relevant work, heterogeneity across topics/stimuli/outcomes, and infrequent study of some uncertainty types (scientific uncertainty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret single-study or small-sample effects cautiously; account for publication bias and heterogeneity in syntheses; expand methods and taxa of study to reduce blind spots (visual representations, interpersonal contexts, multi-message sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for future research design
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested future directions: identify conditional moderators more precisely; apply different typologies of uncertainty (e.g., Funtowicz & Ravetz, van der Bles et al.); assess topic–uncertainty type associations; test combinations or sequences of uncertainty types; include visual depictions of uncertainty and broader contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to test interactions and boundary conditions, use larger and representative samples, pre-register analyses, and broaden operationalizations of uncertainty to improve generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental manipulation constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Review inclusion required that uncertainty manipulations be presented within a single message and measured as such; studies presenting uncertainty via multiple or sequential messages were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing uncertainty effects, ensure manipulations are contained within the treatment message if the research question focuses on single-message effects; if testing cumulative or sequential messaging, explicitly design for that and note differences from single-message findings.
